subject: physics
prompt: Meera starts at the reference point **O** and jogs **70 m** in the positive direction. She then turns and jogs **40 m** back along the same track. Tap her **final position**.

image.alt: A straight track marked as a number line, with numbered markers

hint: Count forward as + and backward as −, then add.
explanation: Her final position is $+70\ \text{m} - 40\ \text{m} = +30\ \text{m}$: 30 m on the positive side of O. So her **displacement** is 30 m in the positive direction, while the **total distance** she ran is 70 + 40 = 110 m. The +70 m mark forgets the return leg, and +110 m adds the two legs as if she never turned back.

prompt: A toy robot starts at the **+40 m** mark on this track. Over the next minute its **displacement** is **−80 m**. Tap where the robot ends up.

image.alt: A straight track marked as a number line, with numbered markers

hint: Final position = starting position + displacement. Watch the sign.
explanation: Final position = $+40\ \text{m} + (-80\ \text{m}) = -40\ \text{m}$, which is 40 m on the **negative** side of O. The minus sign of the displacement means the robot moved in the negative direction. Choosing −80 m treats the displacement as the final position, and +120 m ignores the minus sign.

subject: physics
prompt: The position–time graph shows a scooter on a straight road. Tap the part of the graph where the scooter is **at rest**.

image.alt: A position-time graph of a scooter with numbered markers

hint: If the position does not change with time, what does the line look like?
explanation: From 2 s to 5 s the line is **parallel to the time axis**: the position stays at 40 m, so the scooter is at rest 40 m from the origin. Its slope, and so its velocity, is zero there. Every other part slopes, so the position is changing.

subject: physics
prompt: Look at the same scooter's position–time graph. Tap the part where the scooter moves **fastest**.

image.alt: A position-time graph of a scooter with numbered markers

hint: The steeper the line, the greater the velocity.
explanation: Velocity is the **slope** of a position–time graph. 0–2 s: $\dfrac{40}{2} = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$; 5–7 s: $\dfrac{120 - 40}{7 - 5} = 40\ \text{m s}^{-1}$; 7–10 s: $\dfrac{30}{3} = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$; 10–12 s: $\dfrac{110 - 150}{2} = -20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The steepest part, 5–7 s, is the fastest. Being far from the origin (the highest part of the graph) is not the same as moving fast.

subject: physics
prompt: Tap the part of the scooter's position–time graph where it is moving **back towards the origin**.

image.alt: A position-time graph of a scooter with numbered markers

hint: Look for the part where the position gets smaller as time goes on.
explanation: Between 10 s and 12 s the position falls from 150 m to 110 m, so the scooter is heading back towards the origin (the negative direction), with velocity $\dfrac{110 - 150}{12 - 10} = -20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. In the rising parts it moves away from the origin, and in the flat part it is at rest.

subject: physics
prompt: The velocity–time graph shows a car on a straight road. Tap the part where the car is **slowing down**.

image.alt: A velocity-time graph of a car with numbered markers

hint: Find where the velocity is getting smaller.
explanation: From 25 s to 35 s the velocity falls from 20 m/s to 0, so the car is slowing down. Its acceleration is $\dfrac{0 - 20}{35 - 25} = -2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$; the minus sign shows that it acts **opposite to the velocity**. From 0 to 10 s the car speeds up, from 10 to 25 s it moves at constant velocity, and from 35 to 40 s it is at rest.

prompt: On the same graph, tap the part where the car is **moving** but its **acceleration is zero**.

image.alt: A velocity-time graph of a car with numbered markers

hint: Zero acceleration means the velocity is not changing. The car must also be moving.
explanation: From 10 s to 25 s the line is flat at 20 m/s. The velocity does not change, so the **acceleration is zero** even though the car is moving quite fast. From 35 s to 40 s the acceleration is also zero, but there the velocity is 0, so the car is at rest, not moving.

subject: physics
prompt: This merry-go-round is seen from above. It turns **anticlockwise** at a steady speed. Tap the arrow that shows the direction of the child's **velocity** as she passes point **P**.

image.alt: Top view of a merry-go-round with four arrows at point P and numbered markers

spots.label: Along the tangent, in the direction of turning
Along the tangent, against the turning

hint: In circular motion the velocity points along the tangent, in the direction of motion.
explanation: At every point of a circular path the velocity is along the **tangent** to the circle, in the direction of motion. Going anticlockwise, the child at P (the right-hand edge) is heading up the page. The arrows towards or away from the centre lie along the radius, not the tangent, and the downward arrow points backwards.

subject: physics
prompt: A marble rolls **clockwise** round the inside of a ring lying flat on a table. As it reaches the top of the ring, the ring is lifted away. Tap the end of the path the marble will follow.

image.alt: A marble at the top of a ring, with four dashed paths and numbered markers

hint: Once the ring is gone, nothing turns the marble any more.
explanation: Released, the marble carries on in the direction it was moving at that instant: a **straight line along the tangent** at the point of release. Inside the ring it kept curving only because the ring kept changing its direction. This is also why the velocity in circular motion is drawn along the tangent. (You will learn the reason in a later chapter.)

subject: physics
prompt: Kabir's family drives **150 km east** from town A to town B in **2 h**, then drives **150 km west** back to A in **3 h**. What are the average speed and the average velocity for the whole trip?

image.alt: A car driving between two towns 150 km apart

options.text: $60\ \text{km h}^{-1}$ and $60\ \text{km h}^{-1}$ towards the east

hint: Average speed uses the total distance; average velocity uses the displacement.
explanation: Average speed = $\dfrac{\text{total distance}}{\text{time interval}} = \dfrac{150 + 150}{2 + 3} = \dfrac{300}{5} = 60\ \text{km h}^{-1}$. The family ends where it started, so the **displacement is zero** and the average velocity is $0\ \text{km h}^{-1}$. 62.5 km/h comes from averaging the two leg speeds (75 and 50 km/h), which is wrong because the legs took different times.

subject: physics
prompt: Sarang swims from one end of a **25 m** pool to the other and then swims **halfway back**, all in **25 s**. What are his average speed and average velocity?

image.alt: A swimmer in a 25 m swimming pool

options.text: $1.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $1.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ towards the far end
$0.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $1.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ towards the far end
$1.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $0.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ towards the far end

hint: Work out the total distance and the displacement separately.
explanation: Distance = 25 + 12.5 = 37.5 m, so average speed = $\dfrac{37.5}{25} = 1.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. He ends 12.5 m from where he started, so his average velocity = $\dfrac{12.5}{25} = 0.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ towards the far end. 0 m/s would be right only if he had swum all the way back; speed and the size of velocity are equal only when he swims in one direction.

subject: physics
prompt: This puzzle is like one from *Ganitakaumudi*, a 14th-century Indian maths book. Two messengers start **240 yojanas** apart and walk towards each other. One covers **7 yojanas** a day and the other covers **5 yojanas** a day. After how many days do they meet?

image.alt: Two messengers walking towards each other from villages 240 yojanas apart

hint: Walking towards each other, how much of the gap do they close together each day?
explanation: Together they close the gap by 7 + 5 = **12 yojanas per day**, so they meet after $\dfrac{240}{12} = 20$ days (by then one has walked 140 yojanas and the other 100). 120 days uses the difference 7 − 5, which would fit only if they walked the same way; 48 and about 34 days use one messenger's speed alone. Speed as distance ÷ time was known in India at least from the *Aryabhatiya* (5th century CE).

subject: physics
prompt: Car makers often tell us how quickly a car can reach a high speed from rest. A car goes from **0 to 108 km/h in 12 s**. What is the magnitude of its average acceleration?

image.alt: A car speeding up from rest while a stopwatch runs

hint: Convert km/h to m/s first: multiply by 1000 and divide by 3600.
explanation: $108\ \text{km h}^{-1} = 108 \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{m}}{3600\ \text{s}} = 30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Then $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{30 - 0}{12} = 2.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. 9 m s⁻² skips the km/h → m/s conversion, 0.4 turns the ratio upside down, and 30 forgets to divide by the time.

subject: physics
prompt: The graph shows a cyclist's position on a straight road. Using the points **P** and **Q**, find the cyclist's velocity.

image.alt: Position-time graph of a cyclist with points P and Q marked

hint: Velocity = change in position ÷ change in time between P and Q.
explanation: Velocity = slope = $\dfrac{s_2 - s_1}{t_2 - t_1} = \dfrac{40 - 20}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{20}{4} = 5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. 6.7 m/s divides Q's position by its time (40 ÷ 6), which is wrong because the cyclist started 10 m from the origin. 20 m/s forgets to divide by the time interval, and 0.2 m/s is the ratio upside down.

subject: physics
prompt: The velocity–time graph is for a scooter on a straight road. What is its **displacement** from 0 s to 8 s?

image.alt: Velocity-time graph of a scooter with the area under the line shaded

hint: Displacement = area under the line. Split it into a rectangle and a triangle.
explanation: Displacement = shaded area = rectangle + triangle = $(4 \times 8) + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times (16 - 4) = 32 + 48 = 80\ \text{m}$. 128 m multiplies the final velocity by the time, as if the scooter had moved at 16 m/s throughout; 48 m and 32 m each leave out one part of the area.

subject: physics
prompt: Use the same velocity–time graph of the scooter. What is its **acceleration**?

image.alt: Velocity-time graph of a scooter with the area under the line shaded

hint: Acceleration = slope = change in velocity ÷ time taken.
explanation: Acceleration = slope = $\dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{16 - 4}{8 - 0} = \dfrac{12}{8} = 1.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, in the direction of the velocity because the scooter is speeding up. 2 m s⁻² divides the final velocity by the time and ignores the starting 4 m/s; 12 forgets to divide by the time; 0.67 is the ratio upside down.

subject: physics
prompt: A metro train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at **0.8 m/s²** for **25 s**. How far does it travel in this time?

image.alt: A metro train pulling away from a platform

hint: Starting from rest means $u = 0$. Use $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.
explanation: $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.8 \times 25^2 = 0.4 \times 625 = 250\ \text{m}$. (Its final velocity is $v = u + at = 0.8 \times 25 = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.) 500 m either forgets the ½ or multiplies the final velocity by the time; 10 m forgets to square the time; and 20 m is the final velocity, not a distance.

subject: physics
prompt: A scooter moving at **24 m/s** brakes with constant acceleration and stops after travelling **72 m**. Find its acceleration and the time it takes to stop.

image.alt: A scooter braking to a stop on a straight road

hint: No time is given, so start with $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, taking $v = 0$.
explanation: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as \Rightarrow 0 = 24^2 + 2a(72) \Rightarrow a = -\dfrac{576}{144} = -4\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Then $t = \dfrac{v - u}{a} = \dfrac{0 - 24}{-4} = 6\ \text{s}$. −8 m s⁻² drops the 2 in $2as$; +4 m s⁻² loses the minus sign that shows the acceleration opposes the motion; −0.33 m s⁻² just divides 24 by 72.

subject: physics
prompt: A car is moving at **54 km/h** when the driver spots a cow standing **40 m** ahead. She takes **0.6 s** to react and then brakes with a constant acceleration of **−3 m/s²**. Does the car stop before reaching the cow?

image.alt: A car approaching a cow standing on the road 40 m ahead

options.text: Yes: braking needs only 37.5 m, so it stops 2.5 m short of the cow
Yes: in the 0.6 s reaction time it covers only 9 m
No: it needs 46.5 m in all, 6.5 m more than the gap
No: it needs 84 m in all

hint: The car keeps moving at full speed during the reaction time. Add that distance to the braking distance.
explanation: $54\ \text{km h}^{-1} = 15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. During the reaction time the car covers $15 \times 0.6 = 9\ \text{m}$. Braking distance from $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$: $s = \dfrac{15^2}{2 \times 3} = 37.5\ \text{m}$. Total = 9 + 37.5 = **46.5 m**, which is more than 40 m, so it cannot stop in time. The first option forgets the reaction distance, the second ignores braking, and 84 m drops the 2 in $2as$ (225 ÷ 3 = 75 m, plus 9 m).

subject: physics
prompt: Use the velocity–time graph of the car shown. What **total distance** does it travel in the 40 s?

image.alt: A velocity-time graph of a car over 40 seconds

hint: Find the area under each part of the graph and add them.
explanation: Distance = area under the graph. Speeding up: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 20 = 100\ \text{m}$; steady: $15 \times 20 = 300\ \text{m}$; braking: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 20 = 100\ \text{m}$; at rest: 0 m. Total = **500 m**. 700 m assumes 20 m/s for all 35 s of motion, 300 m counts only the steady part, and 400 m misses one triangle.

subject: physics
prompt: A truck driver moving at **72 km/h** sees a speed-limit sign and slows down uniformly to **36 km/h** in **20 s**. How far does the truck travel while slowing down?

image.alt: A truck slowing down near a speed-limit sign

hint: Convert both speeds to m/s. With constant acceleration, distance = average of the two velocities × time.
explanation: $u = 72\ \text{km h}^{-1} = 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $v = 36\ \text{km h}^{-1} = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. With constant acceleration, $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t = \tfrac{1}{2}(20 + 10) \times 20 = 300\ \text{m}$ (its acceleration is $\dfrac{10 - 20}{20} = -0.5\ \text{m s}^{-2}$). 1080 m uses km/h with seconds without converting; 200 m and 400 m assume the truck moved at its final or its initial speed the whole time.

subject: physics
prompt: A cyclist rides round a circular track of radius **R = 70 m** at a steady speed, completing one lap every **44 s**. What is her average speed over one lap? (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)

image.alt: A cyclist riding round a circular track of radius R

hint: One lap is the circumference, $2\pi R$.
explanation: One lap = $2\pi R = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 70 = 440\ \text{m}$, so $v_{av} = \dfrac{2\pi R}{T} = \dfrac{440}{44} = 10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. 5 m/s uses $\pi R$ (only half a lap); 20 m/s uses the diameter, 140 m, in place of the radius; and 0 m/s is her average **velocity** over a lap, because she ends where she began.

subject: physics
topic: Distance and displacement in circular motion
prompt: Rohan studies from **2:00 pm to 3:30 pm**. The minute hand of his wall clock is **14 cm** long. Think about the tip of the minute hand during this time. What distance does it travel, and what is the magnitude of its displacement? (Take $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)

image.alt: A wall clock whose minute hand sweeps round

hint: How many rounds does the minute hand make in 1½ hours, and where does its tip end up?
explanation: In 1.5 h the tip makes 1.5 revolutions: distance $= 1.5 \times 2\pi r = 1.5 \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 = 1.5 \times 88 = 132\ \text{cm}$. It starts at 12 and ends at 6, at opposite ends of a diameter, so the displacement is $2r = 28\ \text{cm}$. 0 cm would be right only after whole revolutions, 88 cm counts just one revolution, and 66 cm and 14 cm use $\pi r$ and $r$ by mistake.

subject: physics
prompt: A car is moving to the right and the driver is **pressing the brake**, so it is slowing down. Which picture shows the directions of its velocity and acceleration correctly?

image.alt: A car with arrows for its velocity and acceleration
A car with arrows for its velocity and acceleration
A car with arrows for its velocity and acceleration

hint: When the velocity is decreasing, which way does the change in velocity point?
explanation: When a car **slows down**, its velocity decreases, so the change in velocity, and hence the acceleration, points **opposite** to the velocity, as in R. Arrows pointing the same way (Q) mean the car is speeding up. Zero acceleration (P) means the velocity is steady. The jolt you feel when a vehicle brakes suddenly comes from this change in velocity.

subject: physics
prompt: Ravi's car starts from rest and goes **faster and faster** along a straight road. Which position–time graph matches its motion?

image.alt: A position-time graph
A position-time graph
A position-time graph
A position-time graph

hint: Speeding up means covering more distance in each equal time interval.
explanation: A car that speeds up covers **larger distances in equal time intervals**, so the slope (velocity) of its position–time graph keeps increasing: a curve that gets steeper, like S. For example, at 0, 2, 4 and 6 s it might be at 0, 1, 4 and 9 m. A straight line (P) means constant velocity, a curve that flattens (Q) means slowing down, and a horizontal line (R) means rest. A graph is **not a route map**: a curve does not mean the road bends.

subject: physics
prompt: A girl riding her scooter notices that the **speedometer reading stays constant**. Can the scooter be accelerating?

image.alt: A girl riding a scooter along a winding road, with its speedometer

options.text: No: a constant speedometer reading always means zero acceleration
Yes, if she is going round a bend, because the direction of her velocity is changing
Yes, but only if the speedometer is broken
No: acceleration happens only when the speed increases

hint: Velocity has a size and a direction. Which one does a speedometer show?
explanation: A speedometer shows (nearly) the **magnitude** of the velocity at an instant; the direction is the way the tyres point. Velocity changes if its magnitude **or its direction** changes, so on a bend the scooter is accelerating even at a steady speed. Saying acceleration needs the speed to increase also forgets that slowing down is acceleration too, opposite to the velocity.

subject: physics
prompt: A book lies on a table. Riya says the book is **at rest**. Kabir says it is **moving**, because the Earth goes round the Sun. Who is right?

image.alt: The Earth, with a house on it, going round the Sun

options.text: Both: the book is at rest relative to the table, but moving relative to the Sun
Only Riya: the book is not moving at all
Only Kabir: nothing on Earth is ever at rest
Neither: rest and motion cannot be described for a book

hint: Rest and motion are always described with respect to a reference point.
explanation: An object is in motion if its position **with respect to a reference point** changes with time. With the table (or the room) as the reference point, the book's position does not change, so it is at rest. With the Sun as the reference point, the book's position keeps changing as the Earth moves, so it is in motion. Each statement is correct for its own reference point.

subject: physics
prompt: On a cardboard disc, numbers are written **7 cm** from the centre and letters **4 cm** from the centre. As the disc spins faster, the numbers blur before the letters do. Why?

image.alt: A spinning cardboard disc with numbers near the edge and letters nearer the centre

options.text: Both move at the same speed, but numbers are harder to read
The letters move faster because they are closer to the centre
The numbers move faster, because they go round a bigger circle in the same time
The numbers are printed in a lighter colour

hint: Every point on the disc takes the same time to go round once.
explanation: Every point on the disc completes one revolution in the same time $T$. The numbers travel round a circle of $2\pi \times 7$ cm while the letters travel only $2\pi \times 4$ cm, so by $v = \dfrac{2\pi R}{T}$ the numbers move $\dfrac{7}{4}$ times as fast as the letters. The faster-moving numbers smear out first.

subject: physics
prompt: A class uses an accelerometer app (such as Phyphox) to take readings on two phones. One phone is held on an open palm with the arm stretched out. The other phone lies on the floor. Why does the reading of the phone on the palm keep jumping about?

image.alt: Accelerometer traces of a phone held on a palm and a phone on the floor

options.text: The phone on the palm is moving at a high, constant velocity
The app works properly only on the floor
The floor is moving faster than the hand
The hand makes tiny, involuntary movements, so the phone keeps speeding up and slowing down slightly

hint: An accelerometer responds to changes in velocity.
explanation: An accelerometer detects **changes in velocity**. Even a hand held 'still' makes tiny, involuntary movements, so the phone keeps getting small accelerations in changing directions and the trace wiggles. On the floor the phone is at rest relative to the Earth, so the reading stays close to zero. A high but **constant** velocity would also give zero acceleration. (Such tiny movements are studied in medical research on movement disorders.)

subject: physics
prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from **O**. It rises to **120 cm** and falls back to O. Think about every point of this journey. Which statement about the ball's displacement from O is **always** true?

image.alt: A ball thrown straight up from O beside a scale marked in centimetres

options.text: Its magnitude is less than or equal to the total distance travelled
Its magnitude can be greater than the total distance travelled
Its magnitude is always less than the total distance travelled

hint: Compare distance and displacement on the way up, at the top, and on the way down.
explanation: On the way up the ball moves in one direction, so the size of its displacement **equals** the distance travelled (at 40 cm both are 40 cm). After it turns back, the distance keeps growing while the displacement shrinks: passing 80 cm on the way down, distance = 120 + 40 = 160 cm but displacement = 80 cm upward. Back at O the displacement is zero while the distance is 240 cm. So its magnitude is never more than the distance.

subject: physics
prompt: When a driver brakes, the car still travels some distance before it stops. Which of these make that **stopping distance longer**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A car on a misty road approaching a cow

options.text: A higher speed when the brakes are applied
The colour of the car's paint
A tired or distracted driver who reacts more slowly

hint: Think about the speed, the grip between the tyres and the road, and how quickly the driver reacts.
explanation: Stopping distance depends on the **speed** when the brakes are applied, the **road surface**, the **braking capacity** (how large a negative acceleration the brakes and tyres can give) and the driver's **reaction time**, during which the car keeps moving at full speed. Worn tyres grip less, so braking is weaker. Paint colour and horn loudness do not change the motion. Vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communication, being developed in India and other countries, lets vehicles exchange signals and warn drivers of possible collisions.

subject: physics
prompt: Which of these quantities need both a value (magnitude) and a **direction** to be fully described? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A straight track marked as a number line with + and − directions

hint: On a straight track, which quantities carry a + or − sign?
explanation: **Displacement**, **velocity** and **acceleration** must have a direction; on a straight line it is shown by a + or − sign. Such quantities are called **vectors**. Distance travelled, speed and time interval need only a numerical value with units, so they are **scalars**.

subject: physics
prompt: The graph shows the positions of two objects, **A** and **B**, moving along the same straight line for 10 s. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

image.alt: Position-time graphs of two objects A and B over 10 seconds

options.text: Their average velocities over the 10 s are equal
Their average speeds over the 10 s are equal
A's average speed is lower than B's, because A covers a shorter distance in the same time
A's average speed is greater than B's
B travels a total distance of 120 m

hint: Compare where each object starts and ends, then work out how far each one actually travelled.
explanation: Both start at 0 m and end at 60 m after 10 s, so both have displacement 60 m and average velocity $\dfrac{60}{10} = 6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. A moves straight to 60 m (distance 60 m). B goes out to 90 m and comes back to 60 m, a distance of 90 + 30 = **120 m**. So A's average speed is $6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and B's is $12\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

subject: physics
prompt: In which of these cases is the object **accelerating**? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A ceiling fan turning steadily, with a dot on one blade tip

options.text: A bus moving at a steady 60 km/h on a straight highway
A car going round a circular turn at a steady speed
A coconut falling from a tree
A train slowing down as it enters a station
A book lying on a table
The tip of a ceiling fan blade turning steadily

hint: Acceleration means the velocity is changing: in size, in direction, or both.
explanation: An object accelerates whenever its **velocity changes**. The falling coconut speeds up (by about $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ every second), the train slows down, and the turning car and the fan-blade tip keep changing direction: uniform circular motion is accelerated. The bus at constant velocity, however fast, and the book at rest have zero acceleration.

subject: physics
prompt: Which of these are examples of **motion in a plane** (motion in two dimensions)? Select all that apply.

image.alt: A footballer kicking a ball that flies through the air in a curve

options.text: The path of a kicked football
A train on a straight track
A satellite moving in a circular orbit
A stone dropped straight down from a bridge
A car climbing a winding mountain road

hint: Straight-line motion is one-dimensional; motion that also goes up and down while turning is three-dimensional.
explanation: Overtaking another vehicle, the curved flight of a kicked ball and a satellite going round a circular path all happen in a flat plane: **two dimensions**. A train on a straight track and a dropped stone move along a straight line: **one dimension**. A car climbing a winding mountain road moves forward, sideways and upward, which is motion in **three dimensions**, like a bird or an aircraft in flight.

subject: physics
prompt: Match each trip with its total distance travelled and its displacement.

image.alt: A walk to a shop, a climb up the floors of a building and a run along a track

left.text: Dad walks 300 m to a shop, comes home for a forgotten bag, goes back to the shop and then returns home
Asha climbs from the ground floor to the 3rd floor, then comes down to the 1st floor (each floor is 4 m high)
An athlete runs 80 m forward along a straight track, then 30 m back

hint: Distance adds up every stretch; displacement compares only the start and the end.
explanation: Dad: 4 × 300 = **1200 m**, but he ends at home, so his displacement is **0 m**. Asha: up 12 m and down 8 m gives a distance of 20 m, and she ends 4 m above the ground floor: displacement **4 m upward**. The athlete: 80 + 30 = **110 m**, ending 80 − 30 = **50 m forward**. The other two options were distractors.

subject: physics
prompt: Match each description with the term it describes.

image.alt: A stopwatch with its hand ticking round

left.text: A single reading of a clock, such as 10:05 am
The duration between two clock readings
The net change in position between two instants
Change in velocity divided by the time interval
Total distance travelled divided by the time interval

hint: An instant is a single moment; an interval lasts between two moments.
explanation: An **instant of time** is one reading of a clock, while a **time interval** is the duration between two readings. **Displacement** is the net change in position (SI unit m). **Average speed** is total distance ÷ time interval ($\text{m s}^{-1}$), and **average acceleration** is change in velocity ÷ time interval ($\text{m s}^{-2}$).

prompt: Each numbered panel is a velocity–time graph. Match each graph with the motion it shows.

image.alt: Four velocity-time graphs with numbered markers

left.text: Graph 1
Graph 2
Graph 3
Graph 4

hint: A flat line means the velocity is not changing. What does a line lying on the time axis mean?
explanation: Graph 1 rises in a straight line: velocity increases by equal amounts in equal times, so the object **speeds up with constant acceleration**. Graph 2 is parallel to the time axis: **constant velocity**, zero acceleration. Graph 3 lies on the time axis: velocity is zero, so the object is **at rest**. Graph 4 falls in a straight line: it **slows down with constant acceleration** opposite to the velocity. A changing acceleration would need a curved line.

subject: physics
prompt: For motion in a straight line with **constant acceleration**, match each problem with the most direct equation to use.

image.alt: A car speeding up from velocity u to velocity v over a displacement s

left.text: Find $v$, knowing $u$, $a$ and $t$
Find $s$, knowing $u$, $a$ and $t$
Find $s$, knowing $u$, $v$ and $a$ (no time given)
Find $s$, knowing $u$, $v$ and $t$ (no acceleration given)

hint: Choose the equation that contains the unknown and only the quantities you know.
explanation: $v = u + at$ has no $s$; $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ has no $v$; $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ has no $t$; and $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$, the area of the trapezium under the velocity–time graph, has no $a$. So each problem is solved by the equation that leaves out the quantity you do not know. All of them hold only when the acceleration is **constant**.

subject: physics
prompt: Match each feature of a motion graph with the physical quantity it gives.

image.alt: A position-time graph with a slope triangle and a velocity-time graph with a shaded area

left.text: Slope of a position–time graph
Slope of a velocity–time graph
Area between a velocity–time graph and the time axis
Y-axis reading of a position–time graph at an instant

hint: Slope is a rate of change; the area under a velocity–time graph is velocity × time.
explanation: The slope of a graph is the rate of change of the Y-axis quantity with the X-axis quantity: on a position–time graph that is **velocity**, and on a velocity–time graph it is **acceleration**. The area between a velocity–time graph and the time axis is velocity × time, i.e. **displacement**. Reading a position–time graph at an instant simply gives the **position**.

subject: physics
prompt: Arrange the steps for plotting a position–time graph from a table of readings.

image.alt: Points being plotted on graph paper and joined into a line

items.text: Plot a point for each pair of time and position values
Choose a convenient scale, such as 5 divisions = 1 s and 5 divisions = 20 m
Join the points to complete the graph
Draw two perpendicular lines (the axes) meeting at the origin O
Mark the values along both axes using that scale
Decide which quantity goes on which axis: time on X, position on Y

hint: You cannot plot a point until the axes and their scales are ready.
explanation: First draw the axes, then decide what each axis shows (time on the X-axis, position on the Y-axis) and pick a scale that uses the paper well. Only then can you mark values and plot the points, and joining them comes last. For readings of 0, 20, 40 … m at 0, 1, 2 … s, the points fall on a straight line, showing constant velocity.

subject: physics
prompt: An athlete runs one round of each closed track at a steady speed. Arrange the tracks in order, from the **fewest** changes of direction in one round to the **most**.

image.alt: Four closed running tracks of different shapes

items.text: Hexagonal track
Circular track
Triangular track
Rectangular track

hint: Count the corners of each track.
explanation: Per round, the athlete turns 3 times on a triangle, 4 times on a rectangle and 6 times on a hexagon. As the number of sides grows, the turns come more often and each side shrinks, until the track becomes a **circle**, where the direction of velocity changes **continuously**. That is why uniform circular motion is accelerated even at constant speed.

subject: physics
prompt: Put the steps of the marble-and-ring activity in order.

image.alt: A marble and a ring on a table

items.text: Lift the ring away without disturbing the marble
Lay a ring, such as an adhesive tape roll, flat on a smooth table
Repeat several times to confirm the result
Let the marble complete one or two revolutions
Flick a marble so it rolls round the inner edge of the ring
Observe the path the marble takes once released

hint: Set up first, get the marble moving, then release it.
explanation: Lay the ring flat and flick the marble so it runs round the inner edge. After a revolution or two, lift the ring without touching the marble and watch the path it takes, then repeat to make sure the result is reliable. The activity shows what a moving object does once nothing keeps changing its direction.

subject: physics
prompt: The graph shows velocity rising from $u$ to $v$ in time $t$ with constant acceleration $a$. Arrange the steps that derive $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

image.alt: Velocity-time graph for constant acceleration, with the area split into a rectangle and a triangle

items.text: Triangle ABC $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times t \times (v - u)$
Displacement $s$ = area OABD under the graph
So $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$
Rectangle OACD $= u \times t$
Replace $(v - u)$ by $at$, using $v = u + at$
Split OABD into rectangle OACD and triangle ABC

hint: Start from what the area under a velocity–time graph means.
explanation: The area under a velocity–time graph is the displacement. Splitting OABD gives rectangle OACD of area $ut$ and triangle ABC of area $\tfrac{1}{2}t(v - u)$. Since $v - u = at$, the triangle is $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, so $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. Eliminating $t$ between this and $v = u + at$ leads to $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

subject: physics
prompt: Arrange these by the **magnitude** of their average acceleration, from smallest to largest.

image.alt: A bus, a cyclist, a car and a falling stone

items.text: A car: $0 \to 20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in 5 s
A stone falling freely
A bus: $10 \to 15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in 10 s
A car braking: $15 \to 0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in 5 s
A cyclist: $2 \to 5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in 2 s

hint: Use $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$ for each, and ignore the sign when comparing sizes.
explanation: Using $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$: bus $\dfrac{5}{10} = 0.5$, cyclist $\dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5$, braking car $\dfrac{0 - 15}{5} = -3$ (magnitude 3), car $\dfrac{20}{5} = 4$, and the freely falling stone $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. The braking car's minus sign only shows that its acceleration is opposite to its velocity.

subject: physics
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A coconut falling from a palm tree, with its velocity marked every second

assertion: The velocity of a coconut falling freely from a tree increases by about $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ every second.
reason: A freely falling object moves with a constant acceleration, $g \approx 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, due to the Earth's gravitational force.
hint: Look at how the velocity changes in each second.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. The velocities 0, 9.8, 19.6 and 29.4 m/s at 0, 1, 2 and 3 s rise by equal amounts in equal times, so the acceleration is constant: $g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, in the direction of motion (downward). Here downward was taken as positive; you may choose any origin and positive direction, but must keep it for the whole problem.

subject: physics
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Two identical cars braking, one moving twice as fast as the other

assertion: With the same brakes, a car moving twice as fast needs about four times the braking distance to stop.
reason: For a fixed braking acceleration $a$, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $v = 0$ gives $s = -\dfrac{u^2}{2a}$, so the braking distance is proportional to the square of the initial velocity.
hint: Rearrange $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ for $s$ when the car stops.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Braking at $-4\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, a car at 54 km/h (15 m/s) needs $\dfrac{15^2}{8} \approx 28.1\ \text{m}$ to stop, but at 108 km/h (30 m/s) it needs $\dfrac{30^2}{8} = 112.5\ \text{m}$: four times as far. So the safe gap behind another vehicle must grow much faster than the speed.

subject: physics
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A bus cruising along a straight highway with its speedometer needle steady

assertion: A bus moving at a high, constant velocity on a straight highway has zero acceleration.
reason: Acceleration depends on how fast an object is moving.
hint: Does acceleration depend on how fast something moves, or on how its velocity changes?
explanation: A is true: the bus's velocity is not changing, so its acceleration is zero however large the velocity is. R is false: acceleration depends on **how quickly the velocity changes**, not on how fast the object is moving. An object can be moving very fast with zero acceleration.

subject: physics
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A cyclist riding round a circular track

assertion: In uniform circular motion, the velocity of the object stays constant.
reason: In uniform circular motion, the speed of the object is the same at every point of the circle.
hint: Velocity has both a magnitude and a direction.
explanation: A is false: the velocity points along the tangent, and its direction keeps changing as the object goes round, so the velocity changes and the motion is **accelerated**. R is true: 'uniform' means the speed is the same at every point. Uniform circular motion is an idealised model; planets going round the Sun or a vehicle on a circular turn only approximately follow it.

subject: physics
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A car driving from one town to another and back

assertion: The fuel used by a car on a trip depends on the total distance travelled, not on the displacement.
reason: The displacement of a car that returns to its starting point is zero.
hint: Both statements may be true, but does the second one give the reason for the first?
explanation: Both are true, but R does not explain A. A car burns fuel for every kilometre it covers, whichever way it goes, so fuel use depends on the **distance travelled**. R is a correct fact about a round trip, but it is not the reason fuel depends on distance; it only shows why displacement would be a poor measure of fuel use.
